newsitem.title: USA: Cities league - urban leaders 'upbeat' on finances.
newsitem.headline: Cities league - urban leaders 'upbeat' on finances.

text.p: The National League of Cities said urban leaders are the most upbeat they have been in five years about their cities' financial conditions, and urged U.S. leaders to harness that optimism in attacking national problems.

"This is an upbeat, encouraging assessment," Mark Schwartz, president of the League, said in issuing the group's annual report on the state of U.S. cities. "The message to our national leaders in Congress and the Administration is clear: The nation's cities are ready to solve problems. Are you?"

Schwartz said the League asked urban leaders to rate if city conditions improved or worsened over the year, including the economy, roads and other "infrastructure," violent crime, quality of the environment and unemployment.

For the first time since 1990, 60 percent of respondents said most conditions had improved, not worsened, Schwartz said at a press briefing to release the "1996-97 State of America's Cities Report." By contrast, only 17 percent of those surveyed in 1991 saw improvement, Schwartz said.
But now is not time to be complacent, said Schwartz, who said national issues loom that will vastly impact cities.
Schwartz said localities must have a "place at the table" with Congress and the White House on deficit reduction, entitlement programs, and welfare reform.

He said Congress and the White House will heavily influence local fiscal conditions and infrastructure improvements, and urged Washington to give cities a "place at the table." He also said local citizens must get involved, in a kind of "barnraising" spirit.
Schwartz said Washington also will greatly impact decisions on municipal finance, such as tax reform, regulating municipal bonds and surface transportation legislation.

A key problem, Schwartz said, is Internal Revenue Service's recent effort to collect millions of dollars from localities nationwide as a result of alleged "yield burning" by Wall Street in municipal bond offerings.
Yield burning refers to allegations that underwriters overcharged bond issuers for U.S. Treasury securities used in early 1990s bond refinancing transactions.
IRS recently said localities can head off federal enforcement action by entering "closing agreements" with the Service involving hefty back payments.
"This is impossible," Schwartz said, of IRS' collection efforts on yield burning. "We'll have to prove that cities and states didn't violate laws regarding refundings."

The League, which got responses from 469 of the municipal leaders it surveyed, cited five areas where local officials saw the most improvement -- police-community relations (61 percent of those surveyed), recreation (58 percent) economic conditions (55 percent), infrastructure (51 percent) and unemployment (49 percent).
But 30 percent of cities tallied reported worsening conditions, the League said.

Those cities cited cable TV rates and service (62 percent), impacts of unfunded mandates (46 percent) drugs and alcohol abuse (38 percent), youth crime (37 percent) and gangs (33 percent) as declining conditions, the League found.

Cities rated infrastructure, city fiscal conditions, quality of education, overall economic conditions and impacts of unfunded mandates as the top local conditions that must be addressed in the next two years, the League's 38-page report says.
